Punching Down
PUNCH-ing down
verb phrase
A boxing metaphor borrowed by comedy criticism and then by social-justice discourse: to 'punch up' is to mock or rebuke the powerful, to 'punch down' is to mock or rebuke the weak. The frame ranks every act of criticism not by its truth but by the relative 'power' of its target.

⚖️ Biblical Verdict

🔴
Reject
A power-ranking that replaces 'is it true and just?' with 'is the target up or down?' — the respect of persons James calls sin.

📖 Biblical Definition

The phrase has no biblical standing as a measure of right and wrong, because Scripture judges words and deeds by righteousness, not by the social altitude of their object. The law is explicit: 'Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour' (Lev. 19:15). Justice is no respecter of persons — not of the great (it must not flatter them) and not of the lowly (it must not excuse them). Nathan rebuked King David, the most powerful man in Israel (2 Sam. 12:7); but the same prophets also rebuked the sins of the common people (Isa. 1:4). The standard is never 'who is up and who is down,' but 'what is true and what is just' (Deut. 1:17).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A power-dynamics metaphor: criticism is judged by the relative power of its target, not its truth — smuggled into the church to forbid rebuking favored groups and to license contempt for the unfavored.

expand to see more

PUNCHING DOWN, verb phrase. To criticize, mock, or rebuke a person or group deemed less powerful than oneself.

Paired with 'punching up' (criticizing the powerful, treated as virtuous).

Origin: comedy criticism, then broad social-justice discourse; ranks speech by the target's position on a power hierarchy.

Rejected as a moral standard: Lev. 19:15 forbids respecting persons in judgment, whether 'the poor' or 'the mighty'; truth and justice, not altitude, are the measure.

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:15 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."

Deuteronomy 1:17 — "Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's."

James 2:9 — "But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors."

Proverbs 24:23 — "These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment."

2 Samuel 12:7 — "And Nathan said to David, Thou art the man. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A power-dynamics metaphor is smuggled into the church to forbid rebuking favored or 'protected' groups while licensing contempt for the unfavored — the exact respect of persons that James calls sin.

expand to see more

The corruption is the substitution of a power-ranking for a truth-standard. In Scripture a rebuke is right if it is righteous and wrong if it is unrighteous, full stop. The 'punching down' frame replaces that measure with a different one: a rebuke is wrong if its target is lower on a power hierarchy and right if its target is higher. Truth becomes irrelevant; only the relative altitude of speaker and target matters. So a faithful warning against a sin that happens to be practiced by a 'protected' group is condemned as 'punching down,' while open contempt for the unprotected — the conservative, the believer, the traditional family — is celebrated as 'punching up.' # voice-lock-ok: progressive: this paragraph names the punch-up/down framing to rebut it.

James 2:9 names this directly: 'if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin.' The respect of persons the apostle condemns is precisely the sorting of people into classes who may or may not be addressed by the same standard. The world's version sorts by wealth and rank; the 'punching down' version sorts by a constructed hierarchy of oppression; both are forbidden by the one law. The believer who learns to ask 'is my target up or down?' before asking 'is my word true and just?' has already adopted a sub-biblical conscience.

The recovery is Leviticus 19:15 in both directions. The faithful must not honour the mighty (flattering the powerful is its own cowardice, and the gospel rebukes kings) and must not respect the person of the poor (it is no kindness to leave any soul in a sin God condemns). Love does not calculate altitude; it tells the truth to the great and the small alike, fearing 'not the face of man; for the judgment is God's' (Deut. 1:17).

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A boxing metaphor that ranks criticism by the target's power rather than its truth; the respect of persons James calls sin. Scripture judges the small and the great by one righteous standard.

expand to see more

English: a boxing image ('punch up' / 'punch down') from comedy criticism, adopted by social-justice discourse.

Hebrew (concept): the law's lo'-tissa' phenei, 'thou shalt not respect persons' (Lev. 19:15; Deut. 1:17) — the categorical refusal of power-ranked justice.

Apostolic verdict: James 2:9, respect of persons is sin — the sorting of people into classes addressed by different standards.

Usage

"They called the sermon 'punching down,' as if a sin stopped being a sin when committed by the right kind of person."

"Nathan punched as high as a prophet can punch — at the king — and the standard was never altitude, only 'thou art the man.'"

"Justice respects no persons, neither the mighty nor the poor; love tells both the same truth."
